For the congregation, this includes an annual “Mitzvah (translated as a “com - mandment” from God in Hebrew, but col- loquially means a “good deed”) Day” each May when activities have included baking for local rehouses and blood donation drives. Participants also donate time and money to local organizations like Fresh Future Farm, the Lowcountry Blessing Box Project and Neighbors Together. Weinman noted many people who are not Jewish attend the Nosh. About 5,000 visitors are expected to pour into Hasell Street for the 2026 celebration. The event is free to the public, food is available for cashless payment and a large food tent will be laid out cafeteria style. The event also is in conjunction with Second Sunday; Hassell Street is closed for the day. On the menu Weinman recently delivered 500 pounds of cabbage from Restaurant Depot to the KKBE Kitchen that will be paired with a family recipe to make about 1,600 stued cabbages for the Nosh. In addition to this classic dish, diners will nd corned beef and pastrami sandwiches, knishes, hot dogs, bagels, lox and cream cheese, chopped liver, baked goods, challah, matzo ball soup and Dr. Brown’s sodas, a drink synonymous with New York delis. Kugel and stued cabbage dishes are made by volunteers. Meanwhile, a caterer prepares dishes like knishes, chopped liver and chicken soup using family recipes provided by KKBE congregants. Baked goods like babka, black and white cookies, hamantaschen and rugelach are sourced from Green’s Bakery in Brooklyn. Bagels come from Charleston’s own Bagel Nation. The Nosh is more than just about food. Traditional Jewish music and tours of KKBE’s historic sanctuary will be open throughout the day. And for the little ones, the Kid Zone will have games, activities, cotton candy and a Noah’s Ark theme. “It’s an amazing, happy time,” Weinman said. “You can enjoy your lunch, you can enjoy phenomenal music and — if you haven’t — you get to see a historic sanc - tuary in the midst of Charleston. It appeals to those who like to eat, those who like music, those who are appreciative of his - tory and culture. Bring an appetite!” The pre-order form is available on kkbe.org. It’s a message that the no-voting members of the S.C. Arts Commission have frontloaded with ide - ology, rather than the artists in question. Note to the naysayers: That’s not how the arts function in a healthy, open society. And it’s an ominous precedent for erasing the vital truths hardwon by artists, by cutting o the oxygen of anyone deemed ideologically out of step by the very state agency put in place to support all voices in South Carolina arts. Be prepared for more backroom strat - egizing, head-scratching obfuscation and defensively spat “no’s” from this rogue’s gal - lery. Every year, a portion of the event’s proceeds go to Lowcountry charities. This year, the recipients are the Carolyn G. Rucker Nursing Scholarship at the Medical University of South Carolina (MUSC), which was estab - lished in honor of Darius Rucker’s mother, and Rock N Roll Rescue, a Charleston-area nonprot focused on expanding access to music education, including providing instruments and resources to young musicians. “We’ll always have a charitable compo- nent involved with our festival,” Lamble said. “That’s just another wonderful piece of the puzzle of this festival that gives back to the Lowcountry.” Ultimately, Lamble said he and Rucker simply want the people who come to the Riverfront Revival (typically around 30,000 people attend) to get a true sense of the area from top to bottom. “We’re thoughtful about the choices that we make in terms of music and food and art and charitable outlets,” he said. “And I feel like people that travel here come to have a true Charleston experience.” IF YOU WANT TO GO: Festival grounds open at 1 p.m., Oct. 9 and 10, Riverfront Park, 1061 Everglades Ave., North Charleston.
